lore: The bixi carries steles on its back, and a woken Tantai can bear weights no body should; their elders have held a drifting peak by hand while its chains were fixed. They own the craft of mooring and the Ascent Age records of the pillars, they rent both to every clan, and by salvage right they claim every peak that falls in the Floating Peak Continent. Their own peaks ride heavy, low and ugly, and their vaults are full. They hire ground-born miners, chain-smiths and claim guards, and everyone who owes them dislikes them.
name: Tantai Clan
summary: The bixi-blooded clan of anchors and salvage. They moor the other clans' peaks for a fee and claim every peak that falls.
truth: Tantai records say the Ascent Age pillars were built to hold the peaks below the world barrier at high tide. The Armillary Pavilion pays the clan a fortune never to tell the Conclave.

lore: A Ruin-Seekers' Guild token costs ten low-grade spirit stones and a season as a rope-hand under a licensed diver; divers without one are treated as salvage. The guild teaches breath arts, ward-breaking and appraisal, and its charts mark which halls still have live arrays and guardian puppets. It takes a fifth of every find. Its first rule is never wake a guardian, and its second is never be first through a door. It sells array fragments to the Armillary Pavilion at a fixed price and to everyone else at a better one.
name: Ruin-Seekers' Guild
summary: The ruin-divers' guild of the inner coast. It licenses divers, appraises what they bring up and keeps the only reliable charts of the drowned valleys.
truth: The Armillary Pavilion pays the guild to report every find bearing Ladder markings. The guild reports about half of them and sells the rest to the [[Wenren Clan]].

lore: Every roof in Copper Needle City bristles with rods, and the city hums during storms. Its markets sell thunder-struck jujube, Kui-hide drumheads, fulgurite, copper wire and storm talismans, and its guilds sell storm insurance, which does not pay if you were struck outdoors. The Waking Thunder Sect recruits in the square after every storm by asking who was hit. The Huyan magistrate settles hard cases by having both parties hold a rod through the next storm.
name: Copper Needle City
summary: The plateau's market city, bristling with copper lightning rods. It sells thunder-struck wood, Kui hide and copper, and its storm-insurance trade is cutthroat.

lore: The Cloud-Bearing Works's yards fill a karst valley with hulls hanging from chains. Its refiners cut, cure and balance floatstone, and a boat's keel decides how high it can fly and how much it can lift. It teaches artifact refining to apprentices who sign for fifteen years, and it buys floatstone from anyone at a price it sets. Clans buy its yachts, sects its transports, and the Blood-Thief Gate its fast couriers, through a go-between the workshop pretends not to know.
name: Cloud-Bearing Works
summary: A refining house that builds flying boats on floatstone keels. Nearly every sect in Floating Peak that owns a boat bought it here.

lore: The Baize knew the name of every creature under heaven, and a woken Wenren can look at a beast, a Gu, a curse or a corpse and say what it is and what kills it. They sell these namings at the gate of their peak, one question per visitor per year, starting at a mid-grade spirit stone. They call the Armillary Pavilion's star tables arithmetic and say so in public. Their rootless work as appraisers in every auction house in the Floating Peak Continent, and their bestiary is the best in the world. Their peak drifts within sight of the Star Dial, and neither house likes being watched.
name: Wenren Clan
summary: The baize-blooded seers of the Conclave, who can name any beast, spirit, poison or curse on sight. The Armillary Pavilion's oldest rival in the trade of knowing things.
truth: The Baize line came down the Ladder: one of the three envoy bloodlines. The Wenren matriarch has named an outer demon wearing a human face among the Armillary Pavilion's array masters, and is deciding what that is worth.

lore: The Kingdom Without Gravestones began as a deserters' camp two hundred years ago and became a kingdom when the clans found it cheaper to tax than to burn. Newcomers take new names and burn their old tokens, and asking anyone's past is a duelling offense. The king is chosen by lot. Runaway rootless, escaped servants from the peaks and the Smoke-Keeping Sect dropouts all end up here. It makes good bows and bad beer, and its trackers are the best on the coast; the forts hire them and ask no questions. Children born here are the first in their families with no past to hide.
name: Kingdom Without Gravestones
summary: A hill kingdom founded by deserters from the beacon line. Nobody here uses their old name, and the dead get no gravestones that could be read.

lore: Fog-Shoal Harbor is shrouded in fog nine days in ten. Whale freighters moor to its cliff towers and ships moor below, and the Baili harbormaster takes a fee from both. Cloud ambergris, the waxy lump a sky-whale coughs up after swallowing lightning, sells here to alchemists, and one lump buys a house. Shark-folk walk the quays openly on the Azure Wave Palace's business. The taverns hire lice scrapers by the day and pay in copper; scrapers who fall are not counted.
name: Fog-Shoal Harbor
summary: The whaling harbor of the northeast, at the mouth of the Milk-Smoke River. Sky-whale freight, cloud ambergris and sea-clan tolls all pass through it.

lore: The Kingdom Facing the Dawn's young king spent ten years in the [[Jing Capital]] and came home with Jing laws, Jing officials and the Jing habit of registering every child with a spirit root. He invites the Clear Heaven Sword Sect to test them and keeps a Jing envoy at court. Merchants love him; the Nangong's rootless stewards do not. Children here learn the Morning Star Continent's script and sing the Morning Star Continent's songs. Everyone expects a Nangong singer to visit the court soon, and nobody expects the king to enjoy it.
name: Kingdom Facing the Dawn
summary: A small southern kingdom that has adopted the Morning Star Continent's laws, registers its children like the Great Jing and hosts the Clear Heaven Sword Sect recruiters openly. The Nangong are deciding what to do about it.

lore: The Kingdom of the Brine Marsh lives by salt, goats and everything the Armillary Pavilion forbids. Its salt pans hide stolen array plates, its herders know plateau paths no Measurer has mapped, and its royal house takes a cut of every crate. Children learn to lie to Measurers before they learn to read. Twice a century the Pavilion burns a village to remind them, and twice a century the trade comes back. Brine shrimp from the salt pools are a cheap qi food every caravan buys, and the king pays a bounty for Measurer badges.
name: Kingdom of the Brine Marsh
summary: A poor, free kingdom of salt pans on the dry western edge of the plateau. Smugglers' country: the Armillary Pavilion's Measurers ride through in pairs or not at all.

lore: The New Pit Town is tents, shacks and three stone buildings: the Tantai claims office, an appraisal hall and a funeral house. Claims on the crater slopes are sold by the square pace and jumped by night. Floatstone must be weighted with lead the moment it is cut or it floats away, and the streets are strung with nets to catch strays. The market sells picks, lead, spirit lamps and protection, and the guards sell protection twice. Every sect within a month's travel keeps a hall here.
name: New Pit Town
summary: The boom town on the rim of the newest crater, thirty years old and already the size of a city. It buys floatstone, sells claims and buries prospectors.

lore: Breath jade forms where qi-rich air seeps through quartz for ten thousand years, and a palm-sized piece holds a day of air. The Kingdom of Breath Jade digs it under Zhangsun license. The mines are deep and their gas kills a hundred miners a year, so the kingdom pays well and recruits in the lowlands with the promise of a stone of one's own after ten years. Few collect. Miners' children carry lamps underground at eight. The overseers are rootless and the miners ground-born, and a riot every decade or so reminds both of it.
name: Kingdom of Breath Jade
summary: A mining kingdom on the southern slopes of the spine that digs breath jade for the whole continent. Rootless overseers run it; ground-born miners die in it.

lore: Palace raiders were trapped here, and their elder set off a blood array rather than surrender. It broke but never stopped: a red mist fills the valley floor, and anything that breathes it bleeds through the skin within the hour. Blood herbs grow thick in it and are worth a fortune to demonic alchemists, so the Palace still sends small parties across the strait to harvest them. The clans offer a reward to whoever breaks the array's core, somewhere in the mist.
name: Blood Mist Valley
summary: A valley where an Eternal Night Palace blood array broke during a raid sixty years ago. Its red mist still drinks the living.
truth: The core is the elder himself, alive in the mist at Nascent Soul and feeding on whatever wanders in. The Palace harvesters bring him captives.

lore: The Pass Town sits in a saddle just below the cloud sea, and its gates close the only road between the north coast and the central massif. The Zhangsun rootless who run it charge by weight, by head and by realm, and they fine Foundation cultivators who fly over instead, when they catch them. Caravans rest two days here to get used to the air. The town sells breath jade, crane-down coats, cloud-tooth moss and guides, and buys herbs from the gatherers who come down off the ridges.
name: Pass Town
summary: A walled toll town in the one pass across the Ice Spine Range that mortals can survive. Everyone going north or south pays the Zhangsun here.

lore: The Kingdom of the Shade Calendar's almanac is not of moons but of shadows: which peak will cross which county in which month, and whose rent is owed. Its royal shade surveyors are trained by the Geomancers' Guild and are the kingdom's most respected officials. Children learn to tell the peaks apart by their undersides. The kingdom pays four clans in a typical year and is cheated by all of them; it fights back with lawyers and the occasional forged survey. Its queens are chosen from the surveyors.
name: Kingdom of the Shade Calendar
summary: A kingdom in the middle of the drift lanes that changes overlords with the seasons, depending on whose peak is overhead. Its people keep a calendar of shadows.

lore: In the Wandering Peaks the peaks are not moored. They drift north in summer and south in winter on the qi winds, and the shade calendars of its kingdoms change every year. Peaks are bought, sold and pawned at the Peak-Pawn Market, and pilots of the Geomancers' Guild steer them for a fee. The Yuwen clan's Peak of the Torch Dragon's Pearl sinks a few li a year, and its vault holds the Ascent Age dragon pearl that [[Azure Wave Palace]] wants; shark-folk agents and every thief in the Floating Peak Continent have come to look. Clan children who stray below the drift line are taken by the Blood-Thief Gate. Convoys for Morning Star sail from the Southern Crossing.
name: Wandering Peaks
summary: The drift lanes of the southern Floating Peak Continent, where unmoored peaks wander on seasonal qi winds and the ground pays rent to whatever shadow falls on it. The Yuwen clan's sinking peak hangs here.
truth: The drift carries dying peaks southwest, which is why the Broken Ridges is a graveyard. The Geomancers' Guild can tell which peaks are dying a decade before they fall, and it tells the Tantai first.

lore: The fall killed the king, the capital and most of the court, and the survivors crowned a cousin in a tent. Thirty years on, the Kingdom of the Sunken Ground claims the fallen peak as compensation and stamps the claim on every coin it mints. The Tantai laughed. Its young men work the crater as laborers and its young women cook for the prospectors. Its children grow up on stories of the night the sky came down, and on a grudge against the Huangfu, whose rent their grandparents paid.
name: Kingdom of the Sunken Ground
summary: What remains of the kingdom crushed by the Inverted Peak. Its survivors live on the crater rim and claim the fallen peak as compensation, which nobody has paid.

lore: The Jade Grit River cuts through ruins along its whole course, and its gravel bars glitter with jade chips washed out of them. Panners work every bar from the plateau to the sea, and the Armillary Pavilion buys any chip with markings on it. The Academy of the Chalk Line stands on its middle course. Its lower reaches wind between drowned valleys into the Drowned Ruins, where it flows over the roofs of a sunken city at Ruin-Dredge Harbor and ruin-divers follow its old bed out under the sea.
name: Jade Grit River
summary: A river that rises under the central peaks and runs west across the Dial plateau to the inner coast, carrying flakes of Ascent Age jade in its gravel.

lore: A woken Yuwen's eyes shine in the dark and see by their own light; their elders can turn night to day over a valley. They led the Conclave before the Huangfu, and they still hold the vault where the dragon pearl sleeps. Fewer of their children wake each generation, their peak is sinking, and their debts trade at the Peak-Pawn Market like anyone's. Azure Wave Palace has offered a fortune for the pearl, the Baili have offered to broker it, and the Huangfu have offered to keep it safe. The Yuwen have refused all three, so far.
name: Yuwen Clan
summary: The torch-dragon-blooded clan of the south and keepers of an Ascent Age dragon pearl. Once the first clan of the Conclave, now the poorest, and sinking.
truth: The torch dragon was an Upper Realm envoy that stayed after the Severance: the Yuwen are the third envoy bloodline, and the pearl was their ancestor's own. It still answers to the Mirror.

lore: In spring the ridge turns white with nesting cranes, and in summer their molt falls like snow. Zhangsun keepers guard the nests, and an egg thief is left on the ice without breath jade. Licensed tamers may buy eggs; the cheapest costs three mid-grade spirit stones. Snow leopards and poachers work the ridge anyway. This year the cranes are sickly, and the keepers are burning more dead chicks than they have in living memory.
name: Feather-Snow Ridge
summary: A glacier ridge where tens of thousands of white cranes nest each spring. The Zhangsun rookery and the richest beast-taming ground in the north.

lore: The Zhangsun say their ancestor was the crane the first cultivator watched, and their elders live a thousand years. Woken children take to wind and longevity and can ride the great cranes; fewer wake each generation, and the clan now has more elders than children. They hold the peaks over the Utmost Summits and the breath-jade mines below, raise cranes for the Conclave's couriers, and sell crane eggs to beast tamers at prices that would buy a county. They are courteous, patient and impossible to hurry.
name: Zhangsun Clan
summary: The crane-blooded clan of the north, oldest of the nine by their own count. Long-lived, few in number and growing fewer.
truth: Three of the last five Zhangsun children did not wake on their own. The clan bought grafted crane blood from the Blood-Thief Gate and executed the surgeon's family to keep it quiet.

lore: From the Kingdom of the Ladder Augury's hills the Stump stands on the horizon on clear nights, and the kingdom's priests read omens in its hum and in the Mirror's color behind it. The priest-king rules by augury, and children learn the bow to the Ladder before they can walk. The faith teaches that the Ladder will be mended and the worthy will climb it. Rumors that Armillary Pavilion is building it have filled the temples, and pilgrims bring their savings to buy a place on a list nobody keeps.
name: Kingdom of the Ladder Augury
summary: A hill kingdom of the inner coast whose priest-kings read omens in the Stump. Its people bow to the Broken Ladder at dusk and wait for it to be mended.
truth: A Armillary Pavilion agent pays the high priest to keep the rumor alive. The Pavilion wants a kingdom of believers ready to haul stone when the time comes.

lore: Rifts here look like heat shimmer over water and cut anything that crosses them. Some close in minutes and some hang for days, and a few spit out things from elsewhere: shard-world stones, Ascent Age coins, once a living beast nobody could name. Scavengers work the shores at dawn with weighted lines to test the air. Shard stones found here hold a sliver of folded space and sell to refiners for storage rings. The guild's rule is never stand between two shimmers.
name: Inlet of Folded Space
summary: A long drowned inlet where spatial rifts blown in from the Shattered Sea catch and hang. Treasure washes up in it; so do pieces of people.
truth: The rifts follow the Mirror, not the wind. The Armillary Pavilion can predict them to the hour and has never published the tables.

lore: Sikou rootless sit as magistrates in the Kingdom of True Speech's courts, and the woken Sikou come down for capital cases. Merchants travel from all over the Hanging Shade to sign contracts here, because a Kingdom of True Speech contract is kept. Children learn early to say 'I will not answer' instead of lying, and liars are hanged at crossroads. The crown is elected by a council of guild masters, and the kingdom's schools turn out the best clerks in the Floating Peak Continent, which is the usual road for a ground-born child into clan service.
name: Kingdom of True Speech
summary: A kingdom under the Sikou peaks where lying under oath is a hanging offense and xiezhi-blooded magistrates hear the great cases.

lore: Above the last crane nests the air is too thin to breathe and so rich in qi that meridians blister. Foundation cultivators climb it to temper their lungs, and a few come down able to go without breath jade for days. Most come down coughing blood; some do not come down, and their frozen bodies serve as waymarks. Frost-eye orchids, an ingredient in every breath pill worth buying, grow only here, in cracks near the summits.
name: Suffocation Ridge
summary: The highest summits on the Ice Spine Range, where the air is too thin for anything below Foundation and the qi is thick enough to burn. Climbers' bodies stay where they fall.

lore: The Kingdom of the Falling Shadow has lived under the Peak of the Torch Dragon's Pearl for a thousand years and paid the Yuwen gladly while the peak was high. Now its underside is close enough to throw stones at, falling scree crushes a few houses each month, and the Yuwen still collect the rent. The royal family has stayed, out of loyalty or debt, and its children are taught to tell a falling rock's whistle from the wind's. Abandoned villages fill with scavengers, thieves scouting the vault and shark-folk agents who ask strange questions about the peak's foundations.
name: Kingdom of the Falling Shadow
summary: The kingdom under the sinking Yuwen peak. Its shadow grows a little wider every year, and half the kingdom has already moved away.

lore: Shared Roost City takes in half-bloods that both sides want dead or chained, and survives by being useful: the only safe market between the Morning Star Continent and the Beast Court of Ten Thousand Mountains, and the only city where a tamed beast and its owner's prey drink at the same well.
name: Shared Roost City
summary: A free city of half-bloods on the Vast Wilds Continent's northern coast, and the only transfer array on the continent.

ties.why: The Night Bridge runners bring us Morning Star goods and half-bloods, island by island.
A Gongsun widow pays in cores and captives for blades, and the council asks nothing.

lore: The Jing emperors have ruled for 2,400 years by one law: every child born with a spirit root in their lands is registered, tested and, if good enough, conscripted. The sects call it theft and recruit in secret anyway. The Ancestor Emperor, a Deity Transformation spear cultivator, has not left the palace in three centuries, and his descendants are already fighting over who inherits.
name: Great Jing Dynasty
summary: The cultivation empire that rules the Morning Star Continent's mortal heartland: a hundred subject kingdoms, a spear-wielding imperial clan and an army of cultivators.

ties.why: The Gongsuns hold the southwest march in the dynasty's name, under a frontier charter.

truth: The Ancestor Emperor is dying. The palace array feeds him the capital's veins, and he has decided the dynasty can starve first. He reached Body Integration nine hundred years ago, and a body that strong eats spirit veins the way a mortal eats rice.

lore: Sailors hear the roar for days before they see the mist. Old texts claim masters of the Age of the Ascent could walk out along the falling water into the Void Sea itself.
name: The Rim
summary: The Rim: the world's edge, where the sea pours over into the void. Nothing that goes over comes back.
truth: Outer demons sometimes climb back up it.

lore: The Roof, the plateau of the Myriad Sands Continent, is the highest ground anyone lives on; only the floating peaks are higher, and the thousand lamps of the Thousand Lamps Temple burn along its edge. Below it the Sand Sea runs for a hundred thousand li, crossed by caravans between oasis kingdoms. In the middle of the sand, inside a crater a falling piece of the Ladder made, sits Fallen Star City, where the Heavenly Scale Pavilion runs the auction that sets prices for the whole world. Cities of the Age of the Ascent lie under the dunes.
meaning: Ganges Sands: as countless as the sands of the Ganges
name: Myriad Sands Continent
summary: A high plateau of temples above an endless sea of sand. Buddhist monasteries, oasis kingdoms and the world's greatest market.
top: Mahayana (a hidden monk in the Thousand Lamps Temple)
truth: The Sand Sea is spreading. Something buried under it is drinking the oases.

lore: The Kingdom of Hidden Channels's karez run in the dark under the sand, each a line of wells strung like beads, dug and cleaned by hand since the Dim Age. A figurehead king sits in the capital. The Channel Masters, a guild of geomancers and diggers with three Foundation elders, decide whose channel is cleaned first, which decides who eats. Children start in the channels at eight, crawling with a lamp, and any who can feel water through rock are apprenticed to the guild. Collapses kill a dozen diggers a year, and the guild pays the families in water, not coin.
name: Kingdom of Hidden Channels
summary: A kingdom built on its underground channels, the karez that carry water from the Wall's foot for hundreds of li. Its real rulers are the Channel Masters' guild.
truth: Three channels now flow backward at night, west and down. The guild has bricked them up and told the farmers they ran dry.

lore: For tens of thousands of years the sea clans have carried their dead ashore here, and the bones of jiao and sea beasts lie heaped like dunes, white under the fog. Bone carvers pay fortunes for a jiao rib, and alchemists for the marrow-salt that crusts on the oldest bones. The Cold Tide Clan watches the strand day and night, carrion crabs the size of carts patrol the tideline, and in the seventh month the strand fills with things that were never human.
name: Whalebone Strand
summary: A strand where the sea clans bring their dead. Whale and sea-beast bones lie in drifts like dunes, and the shark-folk kill anyone who takes one.
truth: The sea clans also bring the Azure Wave Palace's executed here. Three of the skeletons belonged to Nascent Soul sea lords, and their cores were never taken.

lore: From the Wall in spring the delta looks like a green hand laid on the sand with its fingers spread. Each finger ends in reed marsh, then salt crust, then dunes. Water diviners mark the end of every channel with a cairn each year, and the oldest cairns now stand in open desert ninety li below the water. The marshes hold reed toads whose skins make a calming salve and sand pike that bite through boots. Below the last cairn the river's dead bed runs on west toward the buried cities.
name: Delta of a Hundred Mouths
summary: The inland delta where the Passing River splits into a hundred channels and vanishes into the sand. Every year its mouths close further upstream.

lore: The Kingdom of the White Delta's fields flood every summer with the Milk River's white silt and dry into the richest soil on the continent. The Yu dynasty has ruled for six hundred years by keeping the dikes up and the sects out, and it sells cotton to the Morning Star Continent and rice to Fallen Star City. Children grow up in the paddies and swim in milky water, which outsiders find unnerving. Spirit-rooted children are recruited by the [[Sect of the Passing Crack]] at the harvest fair, and the dynasty takes a fee for each. Kingdom of the White Delta boasts that its river is the only water in Myriad Sands that owes nothing to the Thousand Lamps Temple.
name: Kingdom of the White Delta
summary: The kingdom of the Milk River delta: white silt fields of cotton and spirit rice, the only farmland in the Myriad Sands Continent that never needs the water court and the envy of every oasis.
truth: That boast is no longer true. The Yu king pledged the river to the water court to rebuild the dikes after the flood of 3,089, and the first rent falls due next year.

lore: The lagoons behind the barrier sands are warm and shallow, and the spirit oysters in them grow pearls that store qi like small spirit stones. The Pearl King is whoever owns the most beds, and the throne has changed hands four times this century. Children dive from five, and the best learn breath arts that keep a Qi Condensation diver under for an hour. Fallen Star City buyers grade the catch on the beach. Sea snakes, rival divers and the odd jiao from the open sea kill a hundred divers a year.
name: Kingdom of Oyster Pearls
summary: A lagoon kingdom of pearl divers south of the delta, where spirit oysters grow pearls that hold qi. Its divers hold their breath for an hour and die young.
truth: The current Pearl King took his beds by seeding a rival's lagoon with a blight bought from a Morning Star herb dealer, and the blight is spreading to his own.

lore: Eight roads cross the sand to the crater: from the Roof, the two coasts, the salt flats, the steppe, the Buried Cities, the Withered Rivers and the Last Light Shore. On its floor stands [[Fallen Star City]], watered by the spring that rose after the fragment struck, and above the city the halls of the [[Heavenly Scale Pavilion]], where no blood may touch the scale. Every caravan in Myriad Sands ends here sooner or later. The next Grand Auction opens in the spring of 3,130, and every escort house, appraiser and debt collector between the coasts is hiring. Outside the rim the sand is glass for a season's ride.
name: The Eight Roads
summary: The crater in the middle of the Sand Sea where a piece of the Heaven Ladder fell, and the eight caravan roads that meet in it. Fallen Star City, the Heavenly Scale Pavilion and the Grand Auction.
top: Body Integration (the Founding Scale, never seen)
truth: The crater spring has dropped nine zhang in a century. The Heavenly Scale Pavilion has hired every hydromancer it can find under karmic oaths of silence, and is quietly buying the third of the oases' water rights that Thousand Lamps Temple does not already hold.

lore: Running Thunder children are put on a horse before they can stand and given a bow at six. The tribe breeds horses with a trace of spirit blood that can run three hundred li in a day, and judges a man by his herd and a woman by her horse. Khan Tiemu, a Foundation cultivator of twenty-six with a spear method nobody can trace, took the tribe by killing his uncle in a duel and has since broken or married three others. Spirit-rooted youths used to go to the Gale Camp for training, until the khan fell out with it.
name: Running Thunder Horde
summary: The largest horse tribe of the steppe, whose spirit-blooded horses shake the ground when the horde rides. Its young khan has united three tribes in four years and wants the rest.
truth: The khan's spear method came from an outcast of the [[Valley of Snuffed Lamps]], who wants a horde that will ride up the Roof road one day, and is patient.

lore: When the ice bridge forms, the Kingdom of the Ice Crossing sledges run north loaded with Roof salt, barley and tea, and come back with black-range iron, furs and steppe horses bought at the [[Frost Fair]]. The Shi family rules, Foundation cultivators all, and keeps a hall where Black Frost traders may sleep without being killed; the monks call it a door left open. Children learn the Frost Fair's trade tongue at their mother's knee and are taught to fear ice holes, raiders and monks, in that order. The Kingdom of the Ice Crossing ice-runner hounds fetch Foundation-level prices in Fallen Star City.
name: Kingdom of the Ice Crossing
summary: A principality on the strait whose sledges run the winter ice out to the strait's frozen market islets, where Black Frost traders meet them. Everyone suspects them, and everyone buys from them.
truth: The Shi family's eldest daughter was sent north as a hostage to the [[Eternal Night Palace]] twenty years ago. She came home last winter as an inner disciple, and she has not aged a day.

lore: At noon the gang wind drops into the valley and blows for an hour, and anyone caught in the open is flayed. The ice holds hundreds of bodies, some in Ascent Age armor, all perfectly kept. Corpse thieves climb in every summer to cut out the ones the ice has let go, and most of them stay. The [[Vulture Burial Temple]] monks hold the valley mouth and release every body they reach first. Last summer a thief came out with a sword that cut through a bone hammer, and the price of a guide doubled.
name: Valley of Ice Burials
summary: A glacier valley where Ascent Age travelers and Dim Age monks lie frozen in the ice. The glacier is retreating, and the bodies are coming out.
truth: The noon wind is not weather. An Ascent Age array at the valley head still pulls the gang wind down once a day to guard something under the deepest ice.

lore: The gate admits only Qi Condensation cultivators, because the garden's guardian array reads anything stronger as an invader. Inside are terraces of Ascent Age spirit herbs gone wild for sixty thousand years, orchards of jade pears, a lake of clear water and puppet gardeners who are polite until someone picks the wrong fruit. The gate stays open for forty days. The last opening was in 3,112 and the next is due in 3,142, and the Camel Bell Tribes know exactly which dune it is under.
name: Gate of the Green Garden
summary: A bronze gate in a buried palace that the dunes uncover every thirty years. Behind it lies a shard world that was once a river lord's private garden, and it is still green.
truth: The garden belonged to the lord under the [[Thirsting Sands]]. Its herbs are the only medicine that can wake him early, or keep him asleep.

lore: The shard and the crater's fragment were once one piece, and when the shard passes near, the two pull at each other until a gate opens on the crater floor. The Heavenly Scale Pavilion sells a hundred entry tokens at the Grand Auction, among its costliest lots. The gate admits Foundation Establishment cultivators and below for twelve days. Inside, the stair climbs into a sunless sky, its landings littered with what Ascent Age climbers dropped: pill bottles, broken artifacts and the dead. The next opening falls during the auction of 3,130.
name: The Broken Steps
summary: A shard world made of a broken stretch of the Heaven Ladder's stair. Every ten years it swings close, and its gate opens in the crater during the Grand Auction.
truth: The highest landing anyone has reached has a door in it. The Heavenly Scale Pavilion sells the tokens partly to find out who can open it.

lore: The fair gathers every autumn where the steppe meets the sand, and for a month a hundred thousand people live in felt tents around a ring of corrals. Tribes bring horses, furs and falcons; oasis and Fallen Star City merchants bring brick tea, grain, iron and salt. Disputes are settled by wrestling, and serious ones by wrestling on horseback. The Gale Camp holds its entrance race here, and the khan holds court. This year's fair will be the first since he united the tribes, and the merchants are worried about his taxes.
name: Tea-Horse Market
summary: The great horse fair of the steppe, where tribes trade horses for tea, grain and iron. For one month a year it is the biggest city in the southwest, then it packs up and leaves.

lore: The town sank in an earthquake two thousand years ago with all its people, and none of them left. Its magistrate, now a Nascent Soul ghost, still holds court in the drowned hall and swore fealty to the Court of No Light a thousand years ago. At every low tide the streets rise out of the mud and the market opens: ghost merchants sell drowned silver, old memories and Ghost Way manuals, and the living sell incense, paper goods and news. Anyone still in the streets when the bell rings for the tide becomes a citizen.
name: Fief of the Tolling Tide
summary: A drowned town on the tidal flats, ruled by the ghost of its last magistrate. At low tide its streets surface and its bell rings, and the living may trade there until the water returns.
truth: The magistrate wants to live again and is bargaining with the [[Thousand Puppet Gate]] for an immortal's body to wear. The Court of No Light does not know.

lore: The Worm Mother slept under these dunes through the Dim Age and woke with the tide two centuries ago. Her brood, hundreds of worms from a zhang to a li long, shed teeth that artifact refiners grind into the finest abrasive in the world, and spit pearls of fused sand that hold Earth qi. Camels walk through unharmed; drums, carts and running feet draw them. Dig camps here hang bells on everything and walk with sliding steps. Beast tamers have tried to steal her eggs for two hundred years, and three have succeeded.
name: Dunes of the Worm Mother
summary: The dune country of the Worm Mother, a sand worm two li long at Nascent Soul. Her brood hunts by vibration, and her dunes hide some of the richest buried cities.
truth: The Worm Mother is fleeing, not hunting. Her brood has moved twenty li east every year since she woke, away from the [[Thirsting Sands]].

lore: The Sect of the Passing Crack teaches the Crack-Walking Art: sensing the seams in space and stepping through a rift before it closes. Its senior disciples reach a floating shard in a day that ships take a month to find, and bring back salvage the scavenger sects never see. Disciples train on the Strand of Tangled Space, where the folds are small and only sometimes fatal. The sect recruits at the Kingdom of the White Delta's harvest fair by throwing a coin into a fold and asking children where it went. One disciple in ten is lost each year.
name: Sect of the Passing Crack
summary: A Space Dao sect that rides the spatial rifts of the Shattered Sea to reach drifting ruins before anyone else. Its disciples get rich or vanish.
truth: The founder walked into a rift near the [[Ladder Stump]] and walked out a century later, unaged. The sect keeps her in its deepest hall, and she has never said where she was.

lore: Every morning fog rolls in off the cold current and every afternoon the sun burns it off, and in between the coast's people catch it in nets and drink it. Ships that hug the shore end on the shoals, then the dunes march over them, so wrecks lie in the sand a hundred li inland, some of them Ascent Age hulls. The sea belongs to the [[Azure Wave Palace]], whose shark-folk vassals toll every boat. Wreckers, fog farmers and beachcombers live off what the sea throws up: whalebone, salvage and ambergris, which sells in Fallen Star City for its weight in spirit stones.
name: The Ship Tombs
summary: The Myriad Sands Continent's outer coast on the Shoreless Sea: a cold current, a wall of morning fog and dunes that march into the surf. The only water is fog, and the beaches are lined with wrecks.
truth: The fog is thinning. Fifty years ago it came every morning; now it misses one morning in five, and the Net Mothers have begun rationing without saying why.

lore: The falls run white with glacier flour and can be heard in the City Beneath the Lamps. Water cultivators meditate on the ledges behind the curtain, where the qi is cold and fast; the best ledges are rented by the year from the Thousand Lamps Temple's water court, which holds the river. The plunge pool breeds silver spirit carp that leap the whole height of the fall once a century, and whoever catches one at the top is said to gain a Water Dao insight. Mist from the falls feeds a terrace of cloud-moss that alchemists use in clarity pills.
name: Hanging Curtain Falls
summary: The Passing River pours off the Roof here in a waterfall two thousand zhang high and becomes the river that dies in the sand.
truth: The volume of the falls has dropped by a fifth in a hundred years. The snowfall on the Roof has not.

lore: The Merciful Blade was founded by a Lion's Roar monk who released a captured blood cultivator and watched him kill a village. Its monks carry one saber each and recite a sutra of release before every killing. They take bounties from caravan houses and give the money to orphanages. The [[Thousand Lamps Temple]] calls them heretics and will not light their lamps, yet its arbiters send them names. Recruits are survivors of bandit raids, and training begins with a year of nursing the wounded, so the monks know what they are preventing.
name: Temple of the Merciful Blade
summary: A heretical Buddhist temple whose monks kill. They hold that taking one evil life to save a hundred is merit, and they hunt bandits and demonic cultivators to the death.
truth: Two of the temple's senior monks are the Thousand Lamps Temple monks whose lamps still burn in the great hall. The temple is the arm the Thousand Lamps Temple cannot be seen to have.

lore: Cinnabar is the base of a hundred pills, and the Kingdom of Cinnabar mines half of the Myriad Sands Continent's. Miners cut the red ore by hand and roast it for quicksilver in kilns that never cool, and by forty most of them shake. King Zhu rules from a red-lacquered palace behind a mask of gold; he is said to be an alchemist who poisoned himself chasing an elixir. Children work the sorting tables from seven. Spirit-rooted children are bought by alchemy houses from Fallen Star City and the Morning Star Continent, and a good fire root is priced like a mine.
name: Kingdom of Cinnabar
summary: A mining kingdom in the red canyons, where the walls bleed cinnabar. Its alchemists pay well, its miners go mad young, and its king has not been seen without a mask in twenty years.
truth: The king died nine years ago. His chief alchemist wears the mask and has been trading the kingdom's best veins to the [[Blood Sand Gate]] for protection.

lore: A hundred thousand pilgrims pass through each year, and the City Beneath the Lamps sells them everything: prayer beads, guides, water, indulgences, forged ordination papers. The temple will not police a city it does not claim, so the Lamplighters' Guild does, for a fee. The caravan road from Fallen Star City ends here, and so does the corpse road: bodies from the Roof come down through the City Beneath the Lamps's back alleys on their way south. The Askers start every inquiry in its tea houses. Roof herbs, salt and lamp bronze sell here for a third less than in the sand.
name: City Beneath the Lamps
summary: The pilgrim city at the foot of the Sheer Wall, below the Thousand Lamps Temple. Its name comes from the old saying: it is darkest right beneath the lamp.
truth: The Lamplighters' Guild is run by an outcast from the Valley of Snuffed Lamps. The Thousand Lamps Temple knows and allows it, because a criminal it understands is better than one it doesn't.

lore: The abbey teaches thunder talismans, soul-settling rites and the peachwood sword, and every village on the coast hires its priests in the seventh month. Where the Court of No Light registers a soul and claims it, the abbey sends it onward, and the Court's clerks have lodged eleven formal protests. The abbey pays bounties for corpse drivers' bells and has burned three Society of Corpse Drivers columns this year. It recruits children who see ghosts, of whom this coast has many. Talisman makers come from three continents to buy its thunder paper.
name: Abbey of Settled Souls
summary: Orthodox exorcists of the Last Light Shore who lay ghosts to rest and burn the corpse drivers' talismans. They send the dead on to rebirth, which the Court of No Light calls theft.
truth: The abbey does not know where it sends the souls. Its founder's rite opens a road toward the [[Nether Shard]], not toward rebirth.

lore: Ten thousand caves honeycomb the Wall below the temple, some carved by Dim Age hermits, most by the Kingdom of the Hive themselves. Their children climb before they walk and fall less often than outsiders expect. The Cliff Lord's family has Foundation cultivators who run the ladder tolls; pilgrims pay in water, coin or labor, and one who refuses is not stopped, just not helped. Boys wrestle on ledges a thousand zhang above the sand for the right to marry. The caves catch seepage from the Roof, and a family's wealth is the drip in its back wall.
name: Kingdom of the Hive
summary: A kingdom of cave villages cut into the Sheer Wall, linked by ladders and rope bridges. It guards the Prostration Stair and charges pilgrims for water.
truth: Some of the oldest caves open into Ascent Age halls inside the Wall. The Cliff Lord sells the way in, one hall at a time, to the [[House of City-Openers]] diggers.

lore: The only reliable rain in Myriad Sands falls here, and it grows feather grass from the coast to the edge of the sand. Horse and falcon tribes move with it, flying wind-horse banners printed with prayers so the wind carries their luck. Every decade the sand takes another hundred li of pasture from the northeast, and the tribes crowd closer to the farms and caravan roads. A young khan of the Running Thunder Horde has united three tribes in four years and is courting the rest with horses and threats. Oasis kings and caravan houses are hiring guards and building walls.
name: Wind Horse
summary: The southwestern steppe, where winds off the Shoreless Sea bring just enough rain for grass. Horse nomads, wind-horse banners, stone men on the plains, and the sand advancing from the northeast.
truth: The khan has a [[Heavenly Scale Pavilion]] banker in his tent. The Pavilion is financing his war on credit, against the oasis water rights he means to take.

lore: The Hall judges water disputes for anyone who asks and everyone who doesn't. Its verdicts are cast on bronze plates at every channel head, and a king who opens a sluice against a plate finds the Askers at his door. The judges are incorruptible in the narrow sense: they take no bribes, only donations to the temple, posted publicly by size. Novices learn geomancy, measurement and the Water Sutras, and senior judges can tell a well's depth by touching its rim. The Hall recruits the children of drowned and dried villages, who have reasons to care.
name: Hall of Dividing Waters
summary: The Thousand Lamps Temple's water court. Its monks walk the channels with bronze measuring rods and decide, every season, how much water each oasis may drink.
truth: The Hall is a landlord, not a court. Two thirds of the oases' water deeds lie in its vault under the Thousand Lamps Temple's seal, and its allotments follow the rents.

lore: Everything lost in the strait comes here sooner or later, caught on black coral teeth below the tideline. Corpse drivers row out to harvest the fresh bodies and sometimes do not row back. The reef breeds corpse crabs that grow fat and venomous, and its yin qi has woken drowned things that drag boats under. In the seventh month the oldest bodies rise and walk inland across the tidal flats, and the Kingdom of Grave-Keepers's militia meets them on the beach.
name: Reef of the Drowned
summary: A reef where the strait's currents pile up the drowned. In the seventh month the bodies on it stand up and walk toward the shore.

lore: The Hard Wind is where the Roof's rivers are born and where lowlanders' noses bleed for a month. Above the passes the gang wind strips qi from anything that flies, so even Core Formation elders walk. Herders give their dead to the bone vultures of the [[Vulture Burial Temple]], hang sutra flags in the wind and sell butter to the [[Thousand Lamps Temple]] for its lamps. The glaciers have been retreating since the tide began to rise, and the ice is giving back what it took: Ascent Age cave abodes, a spirit vein at the [[Slope of the Bared Vein]] and frozen dead whose bodies lowland corpse buyers pay for in mid-grade stones.
name: The Hard Wind
summary: The Roof's northwest: the highest ground anyone lives on, glacier ranges where the gang wind of the upper sky blows at ground level. Sky burials, spirit yaks, snow lotus and hermits.
truth: The glaciers are not melting from the tide's warmth. Their meltwater is being pulled down through the rock toward the thing buried under the Sand Sea, and the ice is thinning from below.

lore: The Kingdom of Sweet Springs's springs have never failed, and its royal Ma family has ruled for nineteen centuries by being first in line at the water court. Its spirit melons, sweet enough to calm a qi deviation, sell in Fallen Star City for a low-grade stone apiece. Children grow up among irrigation ditches and learn the water law as a nursery rhyme: the upstream drinks first, the temple drinks before the king. Spirit-rooted children are offered to the [[Gate of Gathered Dew]] or the water court. The Ma prefer the court, because a son in the court is worth a well.
name: Kingdom of Sweet Springs
summary: The richest oasis kingdom in the Myriad Sands Continent: springs, date groves and spirit melon fields at the head of the delta. Its kings rule by the water court's allotment and know it.
truth: A starving Ma king signed the springs over to the [[Thousand Lamps Temple]] four thousand years ago in exchange for famine grain. The family has no idea it rents its own water.

lore: A corpse driver binds a body with a talisman on its forehead and a bell in his hand, and the dead follow him by night, avoiding the sun. The Society of Corpse Drivers crews buy bodies from grave robbers, glacier thieves, bandits and the families of the poor, and drive them south along the corpse road from the City Beneath the Lamps to the City of Evening Light in columns of fifty. They pay tolls to everyone on the road and are killed on sight by the [[Vulture Burial Temple]]. The society recruits talisman makers and Ghost Way cultivators for its binding arts and takes orphans as bell-boys.
name: Society of Corpse Drivers
summary: The corpse drivers. They walk the dead across the Sand Sea by night, bodies hopping in file behind a bell, and sell them at the ports for shipment to the Long Dusk Continent.
truth: Not every body in the columns was dead when it was bought. The elders have a binding talisman that works on the living, and it is their best seller.

lore: The tower's crown stands two hundred zhang above the dunes, its jade walls still warm at night. Four thousand people live in its upper halls and drink from a cistern the builders filled sixty thousand years ago. The ruling Sun family are appraisers who sell digging rights downward one floor at a time; the frontier is now floor forty below the sand, where the guardian puppets begin. The Kingdom of the High Tower children grow up climbing outside walls, trading shards and listening to the floors below creak. A child who brings back a whole artifact from below is adopted into the Sun family.
name: Kingdom of the High Tower
summary: A kingdom living in the top thirty floors of an Ascent Age tower whose five hundred lower floors are under the sand. Going down is forbidden, and every child dares.
truth: The cistern refills itself from somewhere below floor four hundred. The Sun family has never told anyone, because the price of water is how they rule.

lore: Pools of liquid mercury lie on the canyon floor, bright as mirrors, and in the noon heat the air above them wavers. Alchemists pay well for the canyon's natural quicksilver, which has soaked up a trace of fire qi, and the Kingdom of Cinnabar miners harvest it in wet cloth masks for a tenth of what it sells for. The vapor works slowly: first tremors, then visions, then a calm that ends in sleep. The canyon is full of the bones of people who sat down to rest.
name: Valley of Quicksilver Smoke
summary: A canyon where native quicksilver seeps from the cinnabar beds and the air shimmers with its vapor. An hour there brings madness; a day brings death.
truth: A quicksilver spirit lives in the deepest pool and has been drinking alchemists for a thousand years. It is why the vapor brings visions instead of simply killing.

lore: The Terrace is a tower of salt-glazed brick on the pan's edge, and its watchers spend their lives on the roof recording every mirage: where, when and what it showed. They claim the mirages show the past, the future and far places, and sell readings at a low-grade stone a question. They also teach mirage-sight, a divination method for telling true images from false, and every caravan master on the pan wants a Mirage-Watching Terrace watcher aboard. The Terrace is neutral, poor and extremely well informed.
name: Mirage-Watching Terrace
summary: Diviners who read the Mirage Sea. They sell readings of the mirages to caravan masters and kings, and keep the only reliable record of what the mirages show.
truth: Every reading is sold twice: once to the person who asked, and once to the [[Heavenly Scale Pavilion]]'s information desk.

lore: The Gyrfalcon Tribes take chicks from the sea cliffs and raise them as family; a Gyrfalcon Tribes falcon will die for its master, and a spirit falcon at Foundation can blind a cultivator in one stoop. The tribe hunts, trades furs to the fog coast and guides caravans along the shore. Its chieftess has refused the khan twice and sent back his envoy's head in a falcon's hood. Children are given a chick at seven and learn beast taming before letters, and the tribe's falconers train outsiders for a price.
name: Gyrfalcon Tribes
summary: A falconer tribe of the coastal steppe that flies gyrfalcons at foxes, wolves and men. It is the last tribe holding out against the young khan.
truth: The chieftess is negotiating a marriage alliance with the king of the Kingdom of Yellow Wheat, and has told her tribe the opposite.

lore: This is the only coast in Myriad Sands where a living river reaches the sea, and the Milk River's white delta is green with cotton and rice. Caravans from Fallen Star City end at the ports, where scavenger ships from the [[Shattered Sea]] unload Ascent Age salvage that goes back up the road to be appraised. On clear nights the [[Ladder Stump]] stands on the horizon, a black line against the Mirror. The Sea Market and the Mirage Sea to its south together make the old word for a mirage, and travelers say both earn it. This year the [[Seal Watch]] supply ships doubled their orders for pills and grain.
name: The Sea Market
summary: The Myriad Sands Continent's inner coast, facing the Shattered Sea and the Stump: the Milk River's delta, port city-states where camel trains meet salvage ships, and mirages of floating shards over the water.
truth: Some of the floating shards in the mirages over the water are not mirages. One has drifted closer to the coast every year for a decade, and the port families are already arguing over who owns it.

lore: The Cold Tide Clan numbers a few thousand shark-folk under a Nascent Soul matriarch with a jaw of black teeth. As vassals of the [[Azure Wave Palace]] they collect its toll from every boat on the coast: a tenth of the cargo, or one sailor who does not come back. On truce days they trade pearls, sea-silk and ambergris for iron and salt at Whalebone Harbor. Humans who net one of their young are hunted to their homes. They teach nothing to humans, but coast-born half-bloods sometimes swim out to them and are not seen again.
name: Cold Tide Clan
summary: Shark-folk who ride the cold current along the Myriad Sands Continent's outer coast. They collect the Azure Wave Palace's tolls, take a share of every wreck and drown anyone who nets their young.
truth: The matriarch pays the Heavenly Scale Pavilion for news of the Sea Sovereign. She means to be on the winning side when the Sovereign tries to become a true dragon.

lore: The herd's horses sweat red when they run, and a blood-sweat horse can outpace a Foundation cultivator in flight. The stallion, the Red Wind, is a Nascent Soul beast older than any tribe, and has refused human form out of contempt. The herd follows the rains and keeps an old understanding with the tribes: nobody rides inside its range, and it does not trample the camps. A stolen foal sells for a mid-grade stone in Fallen Star City, if the thief lives. The khan has sworn to ride the Red Wind.
name: Blood-Sweat Herd
summary: A wild herd of blood-sweating spirit horses that runs the southern steppe under a Nascent Soul stallion. Every tribe wants its foals, and the stallion kills anyone who tries.
truth: The Red Wind is old and failing, and two young stallions are waiting. A tamer who backed the right one could own the herd.

lore: The black wind comes out of the northeast without warning, a wall of dust a thousand zhang high that turns noon to night. In the gap it blows hardest, scouring stone smooth and stripping anything caught in the open. Herders read the sky and run; caravans shelter in the stone huts the Gale Camp built along the road. After a storm the gap is littered with buried herds and caravans, and scavengers dig them out. The storms come more often every year.
name: Black Wind Gap
summary: A gap in the coastal hills where the black storms off the advancing sand funnel onto the steppe. When the wind blows, it buries herds where they stand.

lore: The Black Yak Tribes move between summer and winter pastures along routes older than the temple, and they reckon wealth in yaks and debts in butter. Children drink warm yak blood mixed with milk from the day they walk, which hardens them enough that Black Yak wrestlers fight lowland Foundation disciples bare-handed. They give their dead to the vultures and kill anyone caught digging up a sky burial ground. They hate the snow lions, which take a yak a night in hard winters, and the lowland corpse buyers even more.
name: Black Yak Tribes
summary: Herding tribes of the high pastures whose black spirit yaks carry iron horns. Their butter fills the Thousand Lamps Temple's thousand lamps, and they pay their tithe in it.
truth: Two clan heads have sold their own grandparents' bodies to corpse buyers and blamed lowland thieves. The vulture monks suspect one of them.

lore: Its name is for the red willow, the tamarisk that grows along the bed, red-barked and pink in flower and the only shade on the road south from the Wall. Caravans use the dry bed as a highway between the Roof and the salt pan, and every few years a storm on the Roof sends a wall of water down it with an hour's warning. When it runs it ends in the Bitter Lake. In great flood years it overflows the lake and reaches the sea, carrying salt and dead camels.
name: Tamarisk River
summary: A dry riverbed lined with tamarisk that runs from the foot of the Roof to the salt pan. Water flows in it only after storms on the Roof.

lore: The Kingdom of Red Salt's lake is so salty a child cannot sink in it, and the cliffs around it are banded red with rock salt that lowland alchemists use to temper fire-element pills. The ruling Duo family are Foundation cultivators who hold the two passes and tax every yak load. The salt men go down to the City Beneath the Lamps every autumn and come back with barley, tea and news. In spring the lake's spirit brine shrimp bloom into a red tide, and beast tamers come from three regions to net them as feed for young spirit beasts.
name: Kingdom of Red Salt
summary: A salt-lake principality on the high Roof where red rock salt is cut from the shore cliffs and carried down the passes. Nearly all the Roof salt sold in the Sand Sea went through its toll gates.
truth: The lake has dropped a hand's width a year for a century. Duo engineers found a crack in the lakebed that hums, and the family sealed it with a formation and told nobody.

lore: For three days the city stands on the salt, real enough to walk into, and its gates open on a shard world of courtyards and empty markets where the goods on the stalls are real and the merchants are shadows. Cultivators below Nascent Soul may enter; stronger auras find only salt. Anything taken must be paid for in a coin of the shard's own, which nobody has, so visitors bargain with memories, years or names. Thieves find the shadow merchants following them home. The last opening was in 3,125.
name: The Phantom City
summary: A mirage of towers that appears on the pan every noon. Once every nine years, on the night the Mirror is fullest, it turns solid for three days.

lore: The Kingdom of Yellow Wheat's wheat is watered by a small river from the coast hills that dies in the sand a day's ride past its walls. The Ye family has ruled for eight hundred years by paying the tribes enough to raid someone else. The new khan wants twice the grain and a princess, and the king has neither to spare, because the sand has eaten a fifth of his fields since his grandfather's time. Children grow up behind walls learning the bow and the plough, and every family keeps a horse saddled. The kingdom pays cultivators in land to garrison its towers.
name: Kingdom of Yellow Wheat
summary: A walled farming kingdom on the steppe's edge, on the last river before the sand. It pays the horse tribes tribute in grain, and this year the price has doubled.
truth: The king has promised his daughter to both the khan and the Gyrfalcon chieftess, and hopes one of them kills the other first.

lore: The Kingdom of Escorts lives by guarding other people's goods. Its forty escort houses, each with a banner and a blood feud, take caravans from the crater to the Buried Cities, the steppe and the fog coast, and the ruling Great Escort House takes a tenth of every contract. Children learn saber, spear and camel before letters, and at twelve they carry water for an escort. The houses bid openly for spirit-rooted youths in the square each autumn. A broken contract shames a whole house, so the Kingdom of Escorts escorts die before they flee, and their widows are paid in the Heavenly Scale Pavilion notes.
name: Kingdom of Escorts
summary: An oasis city-state on the west road whose whole economy is escort companies. Every family has a son walking the roads, and every funeral has an empty coffin.
truth: The Great Escort House sells one caravan route in fifty to the Thirsting Heart Sect, and its own caravans are never touched.

lore: Desert poplars are said to live a thousand years, stand dead a thousand and lie fallen a thousand without rotting, and the Kingdom of the Desert Poplars feels the same: proud, old and drying out. King Yan has borrowed from the [[Heavenly Scale Pavilion]] against his crown lands to buy water upstream at the court's seasonal sale. Half his villages stand empty with their doors left open for the sand. Children learn to dig wells before they learn to swim, which they never do. The Kingdom of the Desert Poplars's poplar tears, the salt the trees weep, are prized for cooling pills and pay most of the interest.
name: Kingdom of the Desert Poplars
summary: The last oasis kingdom at the tail of the delta, among forests of desert poplars. Its river came forty days late last spring, and its king is mortgaging the kingdom to buy water.
truth: The Heavenly Scale Pavilion's water desk knows to the season when the Kingdom of the Desert Poplars's last wells will fail. The loan falls due eight months later.

lore: The army was caught by an early thaw and drowned when the ice bridge broke, and the strait threw them back onto this plain in spring. Iron Bone body cultivators do not rot easily. They lie in the permafrost in rows, and on the longest nights the strongest rise and walk toward the strait, still trying to go home, fighting at the realm they died at. Corpse buyers pay a fortune for an intact Iron Bone body. The Cloister has a standing order to burn any it finds.
name: Plain of Stiff Bones
summary: The frozen plain where the last Iron Bone Great Khan's army died six hundred years ago. The bodies never rotted, and on the coldest nights some of them stand up.
truth: The Khan's body is not here, but his clan's ancestor stone is, under the largest cairn. The tribes in the Black Frost Continent would give almost anything to get it back.

lore: Six hundred years ago an [[Iron Bone Tribes]] Great Khan led his tribes across the frozen strait, and the Precept Watch's walls and watch-monasteries were built from what he left. Now the danger is the [[Eternal Night Palace]]: in hard winters the pack ice bridges the strait, and blood cultivators cross to take herders, monks and children. The ice forms earlier every year. The monks of the [[Lion's Roar Cloister]] train any layman willing to stand a winter on the wall, and the wall pays in pills, so every poor family on the Roof sends a son. The Milk River rises here.
name: Precept Watch
summary: The Roof's cold northeastern shoulder, sloping down to ice cliffs that face the Black Frost Continent across the strait. Watch-monasteries and fist monks hold the coast against raiders who walk over on the winter ice.
truth: The ice forms early because the [[Demon-Sealing Glacier]] is advancing south. The Lion's Roar Cloister's abbot has known for thirty years and has written to the [[Seal Watch]] eleven times without an answer.

lore: The Gale Camp has no mountain and no gate: it is three hundred tents that move every month, and its disciples are born, trained and buried on horseback. It teaches the Gale Spear, a Wind Dao lance method built for the charge, and bonding arts that let a rider share qi with a mount. The Camp hires its lancers to caravan houses and oasis kings at prices that keep it rich and neutral, and recruits at the Tea-Horse Market with a race. The khan has demanded its oath, and its master answered that the Camp swears only to the wind.
name: The Gale Camp
summary: A sect of mounted cultivators who live on horseback and follow the grass. They teach Spear and Wind Dao, hire out their lancers, and will not kneel to the khan.
truth: The master is the khan's mother. She left the tribe when he was two, and neither of them has told anyone.

lore: When the gate opens the well fills with blue light and the smell of rain. For thirty days, Foundation cultivators and below may climb down into a world of lakes and drifting rain clouds with islands of spirit reeds; a Core aura makes the water boil and the gate seal. At the last opening an oasis king paid a hundred disciples to carry water out in storage rings, and the lake spirits drowned sixty of them. Spirit lotus seeds from the islands can turn a dead well sweet for a decade. The next opening is in 3,141.
name: Sky at the Bottom of the Well
summary: A gate at the bottom of a dry well in the Kingdom of Hidden Channels. Every thirty-three years it opens on a shard world made almost entirely of water.

lore: Every pass in the Kingdom of Sutra Flags is strung with sutra flags, and every flag is a talisman: the wind reads the prayers and the wind spirits keep off the road. Children herd yaks, learn to read only sutras, and at six are tested by a monk who asks them to pick their past life's beads from a tray. The Returned Prince rules through a council of abbots, and a Foundation regent keeps the seal until the child is chosen. The [[Thousand Lamps Temple]] will choose next spring. Each candidate's monastery is hiring guards, and one boy has already survived poison.
name: Kingdom of Sutra Flags
summary: A plateau principality of sutra flags and stone villages, ruled by a prince-abbot reborn into each generation. The last one died nine years ago, and three monasteries have found three different boys.
truth: None of the three boys is the reborn prince. The real one is a girl in a Black Yak herding camp. The regent recognized her at a sky burial last year and has been paying her family to keep moving.

lore: The harbor's breakwater is a single sunken Ascent Age hull. On the first day of each month the Cold Tide Clan surfaces under truce, and pearls, sea-silk and ambergris change hands for iron and salt. On other days the town buys salvage without questions and sends it inland on camel trains to Fallen Star City. The Harbor Master is a retired Core Formation pirate, and the only law he enforces is that nobody draws a blade on truce day. Ship carpenters here know more about Ascent Age hull arrays than anyone outside the Floating Peak Continent.
name: Whalebone Harbor
summary: The only real harbor on the fog coast: a town framed with whale ribs and roofed with wreck timber, where sea clans and humans trade on truce days.

lore: The Pure Vase nuns compound the Roof's medicine: snow lotus, worm-grass, saffron and minerals ground for days and blessed for months into pills that can pull a Foundation cultivator back from a burst meridian. Their best, the Precious Pill, contains the Kingdom of Cinnabar quicksilver that only they know how to render harmless. They treat anyone who reaches the gate, monk or raider, and send the bill to the [[Lion's Roar Cloister]]. Novices learn medicine, alchemy and the Healing Sutra, and each spends a winter in the wall's field hospitals.
name: Nunnery of the Pure Vase
summary: A Buddhist nunnery of healers that follows the wall and nurses the wounded of every winter's fighting. Its precious pills, made from Roof herbs and purified quicksilver, are famous across the Myriad Sands Continent.
truth: The nuns have treated three [[Eternal Night Palace]] raiders whose wounds closed overnight and whose blood was the wrong color. They burned the bandages and told only the abbess.

lore: The Vulture Burial Temple monks carry the bone hammer and the vulture whistle. They teach the Bone Release, a Death Dao method that loosens a corpse's last qi so the birds will take it, and they tame bone vultures that can strip a Core Formation beast in an hour. They take orphans as novices and pay herders in medicine. Since the glaciers began giving up the frozen dead, southern corpse buyers have offered fortunes for bodies, and the order now hangs the thieves it catches from its burial cliffs, alive, for the vultures to judge.
name: Vulture Burial Temple
summary: The sky-burial order of the Roof. Its monks break the dead and give them to the bone vultures, so that no body on the Roof can be refined, raised or sold.
truth: The abbot's ledger of released bodies has false lines. The order sells one cultivator body in ten to the [[Thousand Puppet Gate]] and uses the money to buy the rest back from thieves.

lore: The Wall runs from the high northwest to the cold northeast without a gap a caravan can use. Roads climb it in three places, the Prostration Stair among them. Its face is riddled with Dim Age hermit caves and the Kingdom of the Hive villages. Sandstorms break against its foot, and every evening cold air pours off the top onto the oases below, which is why their dates ripen slowly and sweet.
name: The Sheer Wall
summary: The escarpment along the Roof's southern edge, where the plateau drops two thousand zhang to the Sand Sea. The Thousand Lamps Temple's lamps burn along its top.

lore: The House of City-Openers holds digging charters on every major ruin in the Buried Cities, bought from the nomads, the Kingdom of the High Tower Sun family and anyone else with a claim. Its crews include formation breakers, puppet killers and sand-rats, children small enough to crawl into collapsed halls. Pay is a share of the finds, appraised at the company's own hall. The House recruits at every oasis and promotes anyone who comes back alive three times. It hates freelance looters, whom it calls thieves, and the Heavenly Scale Pavilion's appraisers, whom it calls partners.
name: House of City-Openers
summary: A company of diggers, array breakers and appraisers that buys licenses to excavate surfaced Ascent Age ruins and sells what it finds in Fallen Star City.
truth: The House of City-Openers is a [[Heavenly Scale Pavilion]] subsidiary in all but name. The Pavilion owns six tenths of it through three shell houses and sees every find before it is appraised.

lore: The sand here is warm at night and cold at noon, which nobody can explain. Water leaves a cup in an hour and a sleeping body in a night, and a storage ring's water is gone by the time you cross the edge. These dunes do not walk; they stand still while the rest of the Sand Sea flows away from them. Every geomancer's rod points to the middle. The Thirsting Heart Sect goes in to pray, looters go in after the cities underneath, and City-Opener crews have found an Ascent Age causeway a hundred zhang down that runs straight toward the center.
name: The Thirsting Sands
summary: The dry heart of the Sand Sea, where dew never forms, wells are always dry and travelers who sleep wake as dry as paper.
truth: Under the center sleeps the lord of the river cities, an Ascent Age cultivator who sealed himself away as the Ebb began. His preservation array has been drinking the land ever since, and as the tide wakes him it drinks faster. He sealed himself at Body Integration.

lore: The sect teaches that water is a debt the body owes the desert, and its Dry Blood Art collects it: a disciple's touch pulls the water from a victim and turns it into qi. Victims are found as light as paper. The sect raids caravans and poisons the wells of oases that refuse to pay. Inner disciples walk into the [[Thirsting Sands]] each year to pour water on the sand and pray, and most come back stronger. Recruits come from dying-oasis refugees, who are offered water and asked nothing. The [[Gate of Gathered Dew]] kills its disciples on sight.
name: Thirsting Heart Sect
summary: A demonic sect that worships thirst. Its cultivators drink the water out of living bodies, leave mummies behind, and make pilgrimage into the Thirsting Sands.
truth: Their prayers are answered. The thing under the sand gives back a little of what it drinks to those who feed it, and the sect master has heard it speak.

lore: The Gate cultivates illusion arts that ride on real mirages, so its phantoms are as solid to the eye as the pan's own. A caravan that turns toward a mirage oasis walks into a salt marsh, a pit or a camp of waiting disciples. The sect takes the goods, keeps useful people as servants and feeds the rest to its illusion furnaces, which turn terror into qi. It recruits salt-cutters' children who are good at seeing what isn't there. The Mirage-Watching Terrace diviners can spot its phantoms, and the sect has killed four of them.
name: Gate of the Empty City
summary: A demonic illusion sect that hides in the mirages of the salt pan. It shows thirsty caravans a city with wells, then harvests whoever walks in.
truth: Its illusions fail wherever the new mirages appear. Something else is painting pictures on the pan, and the sect master has forbidden his disciples to look at them.

lore: A pilgrim who climbs by prostration takes a year and arrives with a callus on the forehead that the temple honors. The stair is also the Thousand Lamps Temple's entrance trial: a child who wants the outer court must climb it without stopping, while monks watch from the top. Every three hundredth step holds a shrine with a water bowl that the Kingdom of the Hive refill for a fee. Cultivators who fly past the stair are not refused at the top, but they are always given the worst cells.
name: Stair of Prostrations
summary: The pilgrim stair up the Sheer Wall to the Thousand Lamps Temple: thirty thousand steps cut into the rock. The devout climb it by lying full length on every step.

lore: The caravan road from Fallen Star City to the coast threads the Withered Rivers's canyons for twenty days, and each day's stretch is named for the way someone died on it. The canyons stay dry for years, then run full in an hour after a storm on the Roof. The red rock bleeds cinnabar, which alchemists need and miners die of. The [[Blood Sand Gate]] robs the road, the heretic monks of the [[Temple of the Merciful Blade]] hunt the Blood Sand Gate, and the caravan houses pay both. In the Milk River Gorge, cliff villages ferry caravans across on rope bridges and charge whatever the river's mood allows.
name: The Withered Rivers
summary: Red badlands between the Roof and the inner coast, cut by a hundred dry canyons and one living one, the Milk River Gorge. Cinnabar mines, flash floods, bandit sects and the road to the sea.
truth: Half the Ascent Age relics sold at the Grand Auction pass through the Withered Rivers on their way west, and a third of all of them were made here.

lore: When the Tamarisk River runs at all, it runs here, and the lake swells for a season before shrinking back to a pink brine pool. Spirit salt crystals the size of fists grow on its bed, prized by alchemists as a preservative and by array makers as a qi conductor. Pink cranes wade the shallows eating the shrimp, and their feathers sell as talisman brushes. Swimming is easy; drinking is death.
name: The Bitter Lake
summary: The bitter lake where the Tamarisk River ends, in the middle of the salt pan. Its brine grows spirit salt crystals, and its shores are pink with brine shrimp.

lore: The elder came here after his term at the Stump, sat on the headland for sixty years watching the Pillar, and carved one stele before he died. It holds a Space Dao insight and a column of numbers nobody has understood. Cultivators come to sit before it; most get a headache and a few break through. Pilgrims leave water bowls for his ghost, which is said to stand at the edge on nights when the Stump hums.
name: Ladder-Gazing Cliff
summary: A headland from which the Stump can be seen on clear nights. A Dao stele on its tip was carved by a Seal Watch elder who never went back to his post.
truth: The numbers are dates: the years the seal weakened most. All but the last have already happened, and the last is less than ten years away.

lore: The Kingdom of Linked Forts's kings are lay disciples of the [[Lion's Roar Cloister]] and rule from the bell-fort. Children learn to read ice before letters: grey ice holds, white ice lies, black ice is the sea waiting. The wall bells ring a code everyone knows from birth, one stroke for fog, three for raiders, nine for the ice bridge. When the bridge forms, the villages empty into the forts. Spirit-rooted boys go to the Cloister; spirit-rooted girls go to the forts' archer schools, which fight from the wall with talisman arrows.
name: Kingdom of Linked Forts
summary: A mortal kingdom of forts strung along the ice cliffs, joined by a wall built after the last Iron Bone invasion. Every boy serves three winters on it.
truth: The king pays the [[Eternal Night Palace]] a yearly tribute of twenty mortals to spare his own fort. The villages chosen believe raiders took them.

lore: No single merchant can afford to cross the Sand Sea alone, so the Lead Camels organize convoys of a thousand beasts and sell space by the pack. A guild caravan carries water, guards, a geomancer and a Heavenly Scale Pavilion clerk, and its departure dates are posted in every oasis a year ahead. The guild hires the Kingdom of Escorts escorts, buys water at a discount and blacklists oases that overcharge. Caravan masters serve a seven-year apprenticeship that starts with mucking out camels and ends with a solo crossing. The guild's old enemy is the Thirsting Heart Sect, which it pays anyway.
name: Guild of Lead Camels
summary: The caravan masters' guild of the eight roads. It schedules the great caravans, sells places in them and decides which roads are open, which is to say which kingdoms eat.
truth: The guild has quietly stopped routing caravans through four western oases. It knows their wells will fail within a decade, and would rather they die without its trade than with it.

lore: For a season's ride beyond the rim the sand was melted into green glass, now cracked into plates and hidden under a skin of drift. Where the drift blows away, the glass lenses noon light into points that can set a camel alight. Caravans cross before dawn or after dusk on the marked roads. Glass scorpions, clear and nearly invisible, nest in the cracks, and their venom goes into clarity pills. Off the roads the glass holds bubbles of Ascent Age air, which alchemists buy by the jar.
name: The Glass Plain
summary: The plain of glass around the crater, made when the fragment struck. At noon it focuses the sun and burns travelers alive; at night it sings as it cools.

lore: The fog coast's richest beach is a crescent of grey sand below the dunes, where storms bring in ambergris from the beasts of the deep trenches. After every winter gale, villagers, wreckers and passing cultivators race to the strand at first light, and the beach rule is simple: whoever's hand is on a lump owns it, and hands can be removed. Spirit ambergris from beasts at Core Formation or above burns with a scent that calms the heart demon and is worth ten times as much. When the sea clans come ashore for the biggest lumps, nobody argues.
name: Ambergris Strand
summary: A beach where the cold current drops ambergris after winter storms. A lump the size of a head sells in Fallen Star City for mid-grade stones, and claims are settled with knives.

lore: The rift closed, but the folds it left still shift with the tides. Footprints stop mid-stride, and a shout comes back from behind you. Things from the Shattered Sea wash up through the folds: Ascent Age debris, sea beasts far from home, sometimes the bodies of salvagers lost a thousand li away. The Sect of the Passing Crack disciples train here because the folds are small. The Harbor of Camels and Sails salvagers pay children to comb the edges at low tide, and pay their parents when they do not come back.
name: Strand of Tangled Space
summary: A stretch of shore where a spatial rift came ashore three hundred years ago and never fully left. Space here is folded: a step can carry you ten li, or into the sea.

lore: The vein runs out of the moraine like a seam of blue fire, and the qi above it is the richest on the Roof outside the Thousand Lamps Temple's halls. Nobody owned the ice, so nobody owns the vein: the Kingdom of Sutra Flags monasteries, Black Yak clans, lowland sects and freelance cultivators have all staked claims, and the claims are settled at night. The Black Yak Tribes charge for passage up the only trail. The Thousand Lamps Temple offered to arbitrate and was politely ignored, which it has not forgotten. The ice is still retreating, and every month uncovers another stretch.
name: Slope of the Bared Vein
summary: A glacier slope where the retreating ice has uncovered a mid-grade spirit vein. Three years after it surfaced, a thousand cultivators are camped in the thin air fighting over it.
